subject: Biology
title: Ecology (Part II)
outline: Describe the carbon, nitrogen and water cycles and the role of micro-organisms
Explain ecological succession, both primary and secondary, and the climax community
Analyse population growth, its factors and the concept of carrying capacity
Discuss adaptation of organisms to aquatic and terrestrial habitats
Evaluate pollution, its effects and control measures
Discuss conservation of natural resources and sustainable development

modules.title: Nutrient Cycles
modules.html:
1. The Carbon Cycle

Carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis and returned by respiration, decay and combustion of fossil fuels:

$$CO_2 \;\xrightarrow{\text{photosynthesis}}\; \text{organic carbon} \;\xrightarrow{\text{respiration, decay, combustion}}\; CO_2$$

Burning fossil fuels and deforestation raise atmospheric \(CO_2\), strengthening the greenhouse effect and driving global warming, which causes ice-melt, sea-level rise and shifting rainfall patterns.

2. The Nitrogen Cycle

  1. Nitrogen fixation – atmospheric \(N_2\) converted to ammonia/nitrate by Rhizobium in legume nodules, free-living Azotobacter, cyanobacteria, lightning and industrial (Haber) fertiliser production.
  2. Ammonification – decomposers convert proteins and urea in dead matter to ammonia.
  3. Nitrification – Nitrosomonas: ammonia → nitrite; Nitrobacter: nitrite → nitrate, the form absorbed by plants.
  4. Assimilation – plants build nitrates into amino acids and proteins; animals obtain nitrogen by feeding.
  5. Denitrification – Pseudomonas and other bacteria in waterlogged soil reduce nitrate to nitrogen gas, returning it to the atmosphere.

3. The Water Cycle

Evaporation from water bodies and transpiration from plants (together evapotranspiration) form clouds; condensation and precipitation return water to the earth as rain, where it runs off, infiltrates as ground water or is absorbed by plants.

4. Importance of Decomposers

Without saprophytic bacteria and fungi, nutrients would remain locked in dead bodies. Decomposers release carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulphur back to the soil and atmosphere, sustaining producers and hence all food chains.

examples.q: Explain why farmers plant legumes in rotation with cereals.
examples.a: Legume roots bear nodules containing Rhizobium, which fixes atmospheric nitrogen into compounds the plant can use. When the legume residues decay they enrich the soil with nitrogen, restoring fertility depleted by nitrogen-hungry cereals and reducing the need for fertiliser.

examples.q: Why is waterlogging harmful to soil fertility?
examples.a: Waterlogged soil lacks oxygen, so aerobic nitrifying bacteria are inhibited while anaerobic denitrifying bacteria such as Pseudomonas thrive and convert nitrate to nitrogen gas. Nitrogen is thus lost to the atmosphere and root respiration is also impaired.

modules.title: Succession, Populations and Adaptation
modules.html:
1. Ecological Succession

Succession is the orderly, progressive replacement of one community by another until a stable climax community is reached.

  • Primary succession begins on bare, lifeless surfaces such as new rock or a new pond. Pioneer species (lichens on rock; algae in water) weather the substratum and add humus, allowing mosses, herbs, shrubs and finally trees to establish.
  • Secondary succession occurs where a community has been destroyed (farmland, burnt bush) but soil remains, so it is faster.

Through succession, soil depth, humus, species diversity, biomass and stability all increase.

2. Population Studies

Population size changes according to:

$$\Delta N = (\text{births} + \text{immigration}) - (\text{deaths} + \text{emigration})$$

Population density \( = \dfrac{\text{number of individuals}}{\text{area or volume}} \). A growth curve typically shows a lag phase, an exponential (log) phase, and then a stationary phase set by the carrying capacity of the environment, where limiting factors — food, space, disease, predation, accumulation of waste — balance reproduction. Human population growth in developing countries is high because of high birth rates and falling death rates from improved health care.

3. Adaptation to Habitats

HabitatAdaptations
Aquatic (fish)Streamlined body, gills, scales and mucus, swim bladder, fins, lateral line
Marsh/mangroveBreathing roots (pneumatophores), stilt roots, viviparous germination, salt tolerance
Desert (xerophytes)Thick cuticle, sunken stomata, reduced or spiny leaves, succulent stems, deep roots
Desert animalsNocturnal habit, concentrated urine, dry faeces, water storage, burrowing
Rainforest plantsButtress roots, drip tips, lianas and epiphytes reaching light

examples.q: Describe the stages of succession on a bare rock surface.
examples.a: Lichens (pioneers) colonise, secreting acids that weather the rock; their death adds humus. Mosses follow, retaining more water and soil; then grasses and herbs, then shrubs, and finally trees form the climax forest. Each stage (sere) modifies the environment, making it suitable for the next and often unsuitable for itself.

examples.q: A population of 400 rats in 200 m² records 60 births, 20 deaths, 10 immigrants and 30 emigrants in a year. Find the new size and the density.
examples.a: \( \Delta N = (60 + 10) - (20 + 30) = 20 \), so the new population is 420. Density \( = 420/200 = 2.1 \) rats per m².

modules.title: Pollution and Conservation
modules.html:
1. Pollution

TypeSourcesEffectsControl
AirVehicle exhaust, industry, bush burning, gas flaringRespiratory disease, acid rain, global warming, ozone depletionCatalytic converters, cleaner fuels, tree planting, laws
WaterSewage, oil spills, fertiliser and pesticide run-off, industrial effluentEutrophication, death of aquatic life, water-borne diseaseTreatment of effluent, buffer strips, oil-spill regulation
SoilRefuse dumps, agrochemicals, miningLoss of fertility, toxic crops, leaching to ground waterComposting, controlled agrochemical use, land reclamation
NoiseGenerators, traffic, loudspeakersDeafness, hypertension, stressSilencers, zoning, noise limits

Eutrophication: fertiliser run-off enriches water with nitrate and phosphate → algal bloom → algae die → aerobic decomposers multiply and consume dissolved oxygen → fish and other aerobic organisms suffocate.

2. Conservation of Natural Resources

Conservation is the wise, planned use and protection of natural resources so that they remain available for future generations.

  • Soil: crop rotation, cover cropping, mulching, terracing, contour ploughing, afforestation, organic manure.
  • Forest: selective logging, reafforestation, forest reserves, use of alternative fuels.
  • Wildlife: national parks and game reserves (Yankari, Kainji Lake, Cross River), anti-poaching laws, closed seasons, breeding in captivity.
  • Water and fisheries: control of mesh size, ban on chemical fishing, dam management, recycling.
  • Energy and minerals: efficient use, recycling of metals, renewable energy (solar, wind, biogas).

Threats to biodiversity include habitat destruction, over-exploitation, pollution, invasive species and climate change; loss of species reduces ecosystem stability and removes potential medicines and crop genes.

examples.q: Explain how oxygen levels fall after fertiliser washes into a lake.
examples.a: Nitrates and phosphates cause a rapid algal bloom that covers the surface. Light is blocked, submerged plants die, and the huge mass of dead algae is decomposed by aerobic bacteria which multiply and use up the dissolved oxygen. Fish and other aerobic organisms then die of asphyxiation — the process of eutrophication.

examples.q: State three methods of conserving soil on a sloping farmland.
examples.a: (i) Terracing or contour ploughing to slow run-off; (ii) cover cropping and mulching to protect the surface from raindrop impact and reduce evaporation; (iii) planting trees or grass strips (afforestation/windbreaks) to bind soil with roots.
